questions.question: Describe the audience for the panic button poster and their reading conditions, explain what is meant by the single message and the purpose, and describe the ten-second test.
questions.expected_answer: The audience is people who would buy or request a panic button for themselves or a relative, including older people, their adult children, carers and neighbours, reading the clinic notice board while queueing, standing in sunlight one to three metres away for a few seconds, many reading English as a second or third language or with failing eyesight, so every design decision follows from those conditions. The single message is one idea the reader takes away without effort, here that help is one press away from any room even when the power is off, with everything else on the poster supporting it and anything that distracts removed, since a poster that says five things says nothing. The purpose is action: the reader must know what to do next, such as phoning a number or asking at the school or clinic, in a form that can be photographed or torn off. The ten-second test pins the poster up, has a viewer look from three metres for ten seconds and then say what the product is, who it is for, why they would want it and what to do about it; a missing answer means failure however attractive the poster, and the test is run with another group because the designer already knows the answers.

questions.question: Describe the stages of designing the poster, the four elements and how each is written or drawn, and the layout principles that make a poster work.
questions.expected_answer: Design begins with six matchbox-sized thumbnails trying different arrangements of headline, image, benefits and call to action, which quickly reveals a workable layout cheaply, followed by a rough A4 pencil layout and only then the finished A3 sheet. The headline is the message in five to eight words in the largest type, readable at three metres with letters at least fifty millimetres high, speaking to the reader's need rather than the product's features. The image is one strong drawing or photograph of the product in use, large, with the product clearly visible and people shown with dignity. The benefits are three to five short lines each beginning with what the reader gets, such as working when the power is off, buttons by the bed, stove and toilet, loud enough for the neighbour and no monthly fee, readable at two metres, with features translated into benefits. The call to action gives the instruction and contact, such as asking at the school office with a phone number and price, in a box at the bottom with possible tear-off strips. Layout principles are hierarchy, so the eye goes headline, image, benefits, action by size and position with top-left and centre read first; alignment on a few invisible lines using a grid of three columns and four rows; contrast of dark on light or light on dark with one accent colour; at least a third of the sheet left empty; and consistency of one or two typefaces and a palette of three colours, with a short memorable product name appearing once large and once small by the contact.

questions.question: Explain the honesty requirements of the advertising code as they apply to the poster, describe the accessibility choices, and set out the evaluation checklist.
questions.expected_answer: The Advertising Regulatory Board's code requires truthful, substantiated claims, no presentation of the product doing what it cannot, and no irresponsible use of fear, so the poster says loud enough for the neighbour to hear, which was tested, not calls the police, which it does not; works during load shedding, which the battery guarantees, not keeps you safe, which no device can promise; and shows a grandmother calmly reaching a button rather than a terrified victim, with every claim traceable to a tested specification and the test record as evidence. Accessibility choices are large type for weak eyes, a headline and benefits in English with a community language such as isiZulu or Sepedi alongside, a picture that tells the story without words, strong contrast for bright sun and colour-blind readers who should never need to distinguish red from green, and price and contact in plain numbers, because the people who most need the device are most excluded by small, clever, English-only design. The evaluation checklist is the ten-second test with another group scored on product, audience, benefit and action; a check of every claim against the specification and test record; readability at three metres for the headline and two for benefits; a bilingual check with a speaker of the second language; and a dignity check of the picture, with results recorded, changes made and a line of evaluation written, the poster joining the diagram, truth table, brief and evaluation as the term's marked project.
